title: Trace Playback & Dashboard Runbook for Regression Triage
content:
Purpose:
This runbook describes a minimally opinionated but repeatable process for investigating performance regressions surfaced by alerts, dashboards, or customer reports. It focuses on using trace-playback + dashboard comparisons + lightweight bisects to get from alert -> reproducer -> root cause -> mitigation within a few hours for typical p95/p99 latency deltas.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to hosted and dedicated runtime clusters and private deployments that run the standard serving runtime agent.
- Assumes traces and request logs are available for at least the last 72 hours and that continuous profiling (flamegraphs) is enabled on candidate nodes.
- Assumes access to canary channels or the ability to deploy a baseline binary for A/B comparisons.

High-level triage flow (short):
1) Intake: capture alert details and timeframe.
2) Quick dashboard check: quantify delta and blast radius.
3) Reproducer selection: pick representative traces or synthetic traces to replay.
4) Playback & profile: run trace playback to reproduce latency spectrum and capture flamegraphs/KV cache telemetry.
5) Compare: baseline vs new build / canary vs prod; identify subsystem with maximum delta.
6) Bisect (if needed): narrow PR/commit window.
7) Mitigate and patch.

1) Intake (what to collect immediately)
- Alert ID, affected routes/endpoints, model variant, region, and timeseries snapshot (p50/p95/p99, qps, error rate).
- Any recent deploys, infra changes, autoscale events, or kernel updates in the last 24–72 hours. Link to the deploy job/CI run.
- Customer impact: which customers/teams are impacted and sample request IDs.

Quick dashboard checklist (first 10 minutes)
- Primary panels to open: global p99 latency (per model), route-level p95/p99, cost per token, CPU/GPU utilization, queue depth, batch formation rate, KV cache hit rate, and GC/pager metrics for the runtime.
- Look for: sudden stair-steps vs slow drift; correlated CPU or GPU saturation; rise in queue depth without QPS increase; sudden drop in cache hit rate.
- If the spike is regional: check region routing & inter-region traffic (smart routing fallbacks).
- Correlate with system events: cloud host reboots, kernel upgrades, driver updates, or node autoscaler flaps.

Choosing reproducer traces
- Prefer real traces from the impacted window that show p95/p99 spikes. If unavailable, pick synthetic traces matching the token length distribution and prompt prefixes that were common during the spike.
- Select a set of 10–50 traces that cover: short (<64 tokens), medium (64–512), and long (>512) sequences, and both streaming and non-streaming paths if applicable.
- Annotate each trace with model name, sequence length, and whether it used function/tool calling or structured output.

Trace-playback recipe (example commands and knobs)
- Basic: run the playback harness against the target deployment or local dev cluster. Use --preserve-timing to simulate real inter-token intervals for streaming cases.
- Important flags: --concurrency to match observed qps, --kv-warmup to control cached KV usage, --seed to create deterministic prompt ordering.
- Capture artifacts: runtime logs, trace spans (zipkin/jaeger ids), full flamegraphs, kernel telemetry (CUDA/NVML for GPU).
- Repeat playback against a baseline build or snapshot to get comparative flamegraphs.

What to collect during/after playback
- Aggregated latencies by stage: tokenize, encode, attention, kernel-run, kv-lookup, network-serialize. (Our instrumentation emits these stages if the runtime build was compiled with stage tracing on.)
- Flamegraphs per stage for hot kernels.
- Batch formation and average batch size over time.
- KV cache eviction/warmup curves and cache hit/miss histograms.
- GPU queues and kernel launch times (for GPU builds).
- Scheduler/IO stalls and lock contention traces on CPU-bound paths.

Comparative analysis (baseline vs suspect)
- Use a diff-driven approach: overlay p95/p99 by stage and look for multiplicative increases in a single stage.
- If attention/kernel times rise proportionally with sequence length, suspect kernel selection or quantization path mismatch.
- If queue depth rises but per-request kernel time is unchanged, suspect batching or scheduling regressions.
- If KV cache hit rate drops sharply, confirm whether cache key format changed (prompt prefixing, hashing) or if a new request routing policy bypassed cache.

Bisect strategy (when to do it)
- Start a bisect when: multiple builds were deployed in the suspect window or when a code change is large and not obvious from flamegraphs.
- Narrow to the smallest commit window that reproduces the slowdown using the same reproducer traces.
- Use binary search across CI artifacts (builds) and keep the same runtime flags and infra profile for parity.

Canary comparison matrix (what to compare side-by-side)
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 total; stage-level p95/p99; batch size distribution; cache hit rate; GPU utilization; kernel time percentiles; memory footprint; tail mutex contention.
- External signals: QPS, error rates, timeouts, retries.
- Business signals: request cost per token and downstream SLA breaches.

Common root causes and evidence patterns
- Kernel regression: flamegraph shows new hot symbol; per-token kernel time increases proportionally with length. Mitigation: revert or pin kernel selection; patch optimized kernel.
- Batching regression: reduced average batch sizes, increased queue depth, and queueing latency. Mitigation: revert batcher change or tune batch timeout thresholds.
- KV cache key change: massive drop in cache hits and KV stage latency spikes. Mitigation: roll back key format change or introduce compatibility layer.
- Scheduling/priority inversion: single thread holding scheduler lock causing tail latencies. Evidence: lock contention traces and long tail in schedule stage. Mitigation: fix critical section, increase worker threads temporarily.
- Resource pressure: OOM/GC pauses or driver-level throttling. Evidence: memory RSS jumps and GC/pager metrics. Mitigation: increase node capacity or patch leak.

Quick mitigation playbook (stopgap)
- If canary reproduces but baseline is good: promote baseline routing or route affected traffic to baseline until patch.
- If kernel/regression obvious: pin to previous kernel or model variant; schedule hotfix build.
- If resource saturation: increase node pool temporarily, enable burst nodes, or cull low-priority background jobs.

Postmortem data to capture
- Minimal reproducer set and exact playback flags.
- Baseline vs suspect flamegraphs and stage-level times.
- Commit range used for bisect and the first commit that made the regression visible.
- Mitigation steps executed and customer impact timeline.

Developer tips and gotchas
- Always validate KV cache keys across builds when doing bisects — tiny formatting changes bypass caches silently.
- When comparing GPU profiles, ensure the same driver and CUDA runtime versions; kernel times are not stable across drivers.
- Small changes in batcher timers can have outsized effects on p95/p99 even if p50 looks identical — always check batch size distribution.

Checklist for sign-off to close an alert
- Reproducer validated and committed to a repro-playbook.
- Root cause identified with supporting artifacts (flamegraphs, traces).
- Fix or rollback deployed to canary and validated with playback.
- Regression ticket updated with references and owner assigned.

Open questions / improvements
- Add a dedicated playback dashboard comparing baseline/canary side-by-side by default.
- Improve trace retention policy to keep more p99 traces for 30 days.
- Add automation that runs a quick playback after any kernel or batcher change during CI.

Appendix: quick commands (example)
- Playback: ./tools/trace-playback --endpoint https://canary.api.redwood.ai --concurrency 8 --preserve-timing --kv-warmup 200 --traces traces/selected-50.json 
- Collect flamegraph (on node): ./scripts/collect-flame -o flame_canary.svg --pid $(pgrep runtime-agent) --duration 120s
- Compare stage stats: ./tools/compare-stage-stats baseline.json canary.json --output diff-stage.csv
